source: Siddiqi and Huang (2011) Sequential Diagnosis by Abstraction
finding: Classic machine fault isolation (GDE style) picks the next measurement by entropy over the set of candidate diagnoses, with unit cost per measurement. Cost of isolating one fault is about log2 of the number of measurement points, which is the half-split bound.
numbers: ISCAS-85 benchmark circuits. Authors observe single-fault isolation cost 'comparable to the log2 of the number of measurement points'. They cite de Kleer et al. 1992: entropy method close to the optimal policy on single-fault ISCAS-85 cases.
quote: isolate a single fault in the system with a cost that is on average comparable to the log2 of the number of measurement points
limits: Unit measurement cost only. Entropy method becomes impractical when the diagnosis set is huge. Pruning to probable diagnoses scales but raises average cost. Second-hand for the 1992 result.
agent_relevance: The program can hold the candidate set and pick the next test by entropy; this is the machine version of half-split. The model only names or runs the test.

source: Siddiqi and Huang (2011) Sequential Diagnosis by Abstraction (abstraction trade-off)
finding: Hiding sub-circuits (abstraction) always helps the compiler but does not always lower the measurement count. Coarse-to-fine search pays an overhead: it must locate the cone, then measure its inputs.
numbers: Diagnostic cost = isolation cost + abstraction cost; the paper builds a cost estimator to choose an abstraction. First nontrivial multiple-fault cases solved on all ISCAS-85 circuits except one flat-structure circuit.
limits: The tutorial-grade baseline GDE computes only minimal diagnoses, so the comparison is loose. Circuits are simulated with injected faults.
agent_relevance: Functional-level (coarse) search is not free. Our agent should pick the grain of a test by expected total cost, not always coarse first.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts: Uncertainty-Aware Planning Enhances Information Seeking in LLMs
finding: UoT wraps a model in an information-gain loop: it simulates answer branches, scores each question by expected uncertainty reduction, and asks the best one. It improves success on medical diagnosis, a car/laptop troubleshooting set and 20 Questions, and shortens conversations.
numbers: Troubleshooting set FloDial (894 dialogues, 153 faults, up to 20 turns), closed-set success, direct prompting -> UoT: GPT-4 43.7 -> 67.3; Claude-3-Opus 48.4 -> 56.2; Gemini-1.5-Pro 30.1 -> 53.6; Llama3-70B 28.8 -> 47.1; Mistral-Large 14.2 -> 30.1. Mean turns in successful cases GPT-4 13.4 -> 7.8; Claude 16.0 -> 6.2. Abstract: +38.1% average success.
limits: Planning depth only 3 steps for compute. Assumes yes/no answers split candidates cleanly. Simplified benchmark. Tables 1 and 7 differ slightly (GPT-4 Common 50.5 vs 49.0). AR-Bench found UoT worse than zero-shot on its tasks.
agent_relevance: Closest published LLM-agent loop that uses a half-split-like criterion on troubleshooting data. Supports keeping the split computation in code with the model proposing candidate questions.

source: Hu et al. (2024) UoT reward ablation
finding: Plain information gain and the paper's own uncertainty reward perform about the same on troubleshooting; the gain comes from simulation and propagation, not reward detail. Swapping a self-judged reward for an entropy reward helps another search method.
numbers: GPT-3.5: FloDial IG 67.9 vs UR 67.1; DX 90.4 vs 92.1; Common 41.4 vs 44.2. Propagation scheme, GPT-4: UoT 71.2 vs 68.5 (CRPS) vs 63.7 (UoT-Max) on Common; 67.3 vs 61.4 vs 62.6 on FloDial. Replacing ToT self-evaluation reward with UR: +5.9% average.
limits: One model for the reward ablation. Differences of 1-3 points are not tested for significance in the text I read.
agent_relevance: A simple counted information-gain score is enough; a model-judged score is the weaker part.

source: Grand et al. (2024) Loose LIPS Sink Ships: Asking Questions in Battleship with Language-Informed Program Sampling
finding: LLMs alone write questions that often waste a turn. Sample k questions, translate them to programs, score expected information gain (EIG), keep the best: with k=5 models match mean human informativeness and at k=10 beat it.
numbers: Grammar baseline mean EIG 0.36. CodeLlama and GPT-4 (few-shot) at k=10 beat the human mean (p<0.001 CodeLlama, p=0.01 GPT-4). 40% (CodeLlama) and 33% (GPT-4) of valid sampled questions had EIG=0 (redundant with the board). Translation validity 75% CodeLlama, 88% GPT-4, 40% GPT-4 zero-shot.
limits: Top human questions (85th to 90th percentile) still beat the best model questions. Narrow game, fixed hypothesis space, exact internal world model.
agent_relevance: One third to two fifths of unfiltered model tests carry no information. A code filter that drops tests which cannot change the candidate set (EIG=0) is cheap and backed.

source: Grand et al. (2024) LIPS: board formats and sampling
finding: How the state was shown mattered: only the textual board beat the no-board condition; the visual format was worse or no better (GPT-4V gave no gain). More samples help but flatten.
numbers: p<0.05 for textual vs no board at k=1 to 20; visual worse at k=1 and 5 (p<0.05). At k=5 model EIG tracks the human distribution percentile for percentile; at k=50 still below the best humans.
limits: Single game, two LLMs and a hand grammar.
agent_relevance: State should reach the model as structured text. More sampled tests help up to about k=10, then gains shrink.

source: Grand et al. (2025) Shoot First, Ask Questions Later? Building Rational Agents that Explore and Act Like People
finding: On Collaborative Battleship (42 human players, 126 games) LM agents ground answers poorly, ask low-value questions and choose weak actions. Adding Bayesian Monte Carlo code for each part lifts weak models above humans.
numbers: Spotter accuracy 92.5% (931 questions); code generation about +13.2 points (GPT-4.1 75.2 -> 90.9; Claude 4 Opus 86.8 -> 94.4). EIG-based question choice: up to +0.227 bits per question; redundant (EIG=0) questions 18.5% -> 0.2% for Llama-4-Scout, 14.6% -> 1.2% for GPT-4o. Targeting F1: Llama-4-Scout 0.367 -> 0.764; GPT-4o 0.450 -> 0.782; GPT-5 LM-only 0.716 with no significant gain. Win rate vs humans Llama-4-Scout 8% -> 82%. Guess Who?: GPT-4o 0.617 -> 0.900; Llama-4-Scout 0.300 -> 0.724. Full stack costs about 1% of GPT-5.
limits: Captain test is 18 boards x 3 seeds = 54 games. Bayes-QMD not run with GPT-5 for cost. Question choice alone added only +0.021 to +0.026 F1, so the gain needs the full stack. Boards as text; fixed noise model; win rates post-hoc paired. The abstract's gain range does not match the per-model numbers I read.
agent_relevance: A counted Bayesian layer lets a small model beat a larger plain one at test choice and cuts spend. Question choice alone is a small part; the update step matters too.

source: BED-LLM authors (2025, ICLR 2026) BED-LLM: Intelligent Information Gathering with LLMs and Bayesian Experimental Design
finding: Choosing each next query by expected information gain, with beliefs updated outside the model's context, more than doubles the success of direct prompting in 20 Questions.
numbers: Average +37.4 percentage points over direct prompting across six models (GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4o, Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.3-70B, Mistral-Large, Qwen2.5-72B) and three target sets (animals, celebrities, things); success more than doubled in over half of the setups and never decreased. Beats the Split baseline and an entropy-only ablation.
limits: Prompt-only is a stronger baseline on movie preference elicitation than on 20 Questions, so the gain there is smaller. LLM hypothesis samples show mode collapse (200 samples pile onto a few famous names). Authors say in-context belief tracking is unreliable.
agent_relevance: Do not let the model hold the belief in its context. Keep the candidate set and likelihood in code. Check diversity of sampled candidate causes because model hypotheses collapse.

source: Mazzaccara, Testoni and Bernardi (2024) Learning to Ask Informative Questions: Preference Optimization and Expected Information Gain
finding: DPO on high versus low EIG question pairs (Llama-2-chat 7B) makes questions closer to an even split and shortens games, so a weak splitter can be taught.
numbers: INLG 16 candidates: success 44.4% zero-shot -> 51.1% DPO; mean questions 9.5 -> 6.3; mean EIG 0.31 -> 0.38. Larger candidate sets: +6.7% and +13.8% success. Concrete targets +12.5%, abstract targets +15.4%. On BigBench success 17.2% -> 31.0% but question count and EIG did not improve.
limits: Closed candidate set, yes/no answers, one 7B model, authors call it exploratory. Negative answers still give more uninformative follow-ups. Training is outside our no-training rule.
agent_relevance: Unaided models lean toward one-candidate (hypothesis-scanning) questions; a split-the-set rule in code should be tested against that bias.

source: Zhou et al. (2025) From Passive to Active Reasoning: Can LLMs Ask the Right Questions under Incomplete Information? (AR-Bench)
finding: On three active tasks (detective cases, situation puzzles, guessing numbers) models gather evidence badly. Tree search, SFT, DPO and UoT gave small or negative gains. More rounds help with sharply diminishing returns.
numbers: GPT-4o exact match as low as 35% on Guessing Numbers; Llama-3.1-70B with ToT 52% vs 8B 53% on Situation Puzzles; SFT scored 0 on GN; UoT worse than zero-shot; proactive CoT marginal gain in SP only. Rounds 5-10 add 7.7% process score, rounds 20-25 add 2.5%; 100 rounds on GN 8% -> 18%. GPT-4o process score 44.0% SP, 51.2% DC within 25 rounds. Judge accuracy 96% (Llama-3.1-405B, SP).
limits: Large hypothesis spaces with no clean yes/no split, so results differ from 20Q-style tests. I read only the first 100000 characters; appendix tables not read. No passive-score numbers in the text read.
agent_relevance: Counter-evidence: fancy planning does not rescue active evidence gathering when the answer space is not a clean split. A boundary condition for a half-split scaffold.

source: Kim et al. (2026) Why Do AI Agents Systematically Fail at Cloud Root Cause Analysis?
finding: Process-level study of 1,675 OpenRCA runs across five models: the top failures are hallucinated reading of returned data and incomplete exploration, not wrong search order.
numbers: Overall perfect accuracy 3.9% to 12.5%. Hallucination in interpretation 71.2% of runs; incomplete exploration 63.9%; symptom-as-cause 39.9%; no cross-validation 18.6%; code generation error 27.2% (1.8% Gemini 2.5 Pro to 65.5% Claude Sonnet 4); max step exhaustion 4.1%. Enriched inter-agent protocol: steps 11.9 -> 9.2 (-22.1%), tokens per step +24.8%, net tokens -1.6%, time -22.3%; GPT-5 mini perfect detections 0 -> 2 (0.0% -> 4.9%).
limits: Mitigation tested on a Bank-domain subset with tiny counts. Prompt engineering widened exploration but did not cut hallucinated interpretation. Logs and metrics, not live hardware.
agent_relevance: Agent fault isolation fails mostly at reading evidence and at covering the candidate set. Argues for code-held coverage of the candidate list and for checking readings with a computation.

source: OpenRCA 2.0 (2026) From Outcome Labels to Causal Process Supervision
finding: Scoring the causal path, not just the named component, shows models often land on the right service without a verified propagation path.
numbers: 500 instances, 11 frontier LLMs. Exact root-cause set recovered in 20.7% of cases on average. At least one correct root-cause service found in 76.0%, but grounded in a verified causal path in only 61.5% ('ungrounded diagnosis').
limits: I read the abstract and introduction only, not the per-model tables. Injected faults in microservice systems, not physical ones.
agent_relevance: Right answer without right path is common. A search scaffold should record the evidence path for each conclusion and be scored on it.

source: Tseng et al. (2026) FaulT-Bench: Benchmarking Network Troubleshooting LLM Agents under Unreliable User Tickets
finding: Three agents (SADE, ReAct, Claude Code) are near saturation on accurate tickets and resist wrong-device or wrong-cause claims, but on healthy networks they keep probing until a benign condition can be named as the fault.
numbers: 200 scenarios, 8 topologies (80 correct-fault, 72 false-premise, 24 wrong-device, 24 wrong-cause). Mean outcome score correct-fault 0.932, false-premise 0.820; wrong-device +2.5 points and wrong-cause -2.1 points vs correct-fault. False fault reported on healthy networks: SADE 24% (51/210), ReAct 16% (33/209), Claude Code 11% (21/198). 8% of (scenario, agent) cells move by 0.5 or more between passes, so three-pass means are used.
quote: they fail by continuing to probe until some genuine but benign standing network condition can be presented as the root cause
limits: LLM-judge grading. Emulated networks with injected faults; about 6 minutes per run. Test order and probe counts not analysed in what I read.
agent_relevance: A search loop without a stopping rule over-diagnoses. Stop when the candidate set is empty or the cheap checks pass, and allow the answer 'no fault'.

source: Tseng et al. (2026) FaulT-Bench: ticket persona rewrites
finding: How a ticket is written matters more than what it claims: a confident wrong cause is handled about like the standard ticket, a vague one with no cause hurts.
numbers: Same 72 healthy networks, mean outcome score by ticket: standard 0.820; naive (confident, names a cause) 0.820; novice-confident 0.714; novice (vague, no cause) 0.675; naive-unsure 0.638; naive with no detail 0.497. False-fault rate for the no-detail ticket 47%, timeouts 22%. Accuracy swing up to 14.5 points.
limits: Extracted table rows; label alignment inferred from the text. Each persona ticket run twice; standard row from three passes.
agent_relevance: Vague symptoms cause wide undirected probing. Structured symptom intake before the first test may recover most of the loss.

source: Chauhan and Pendyala (2026) Benchmarking LLM-Guided Control-Plane Policies for Backend Fault Isolation in HAProxy
finding: Models read telemetry every 10 s and drain faulty backends under guardrails. Pooled over 224 runs, localization is good for models above a size threshold and erratic below it. Recall falls as the fleet grows.
numbers: Pooled precision/recall/F1 0.913/0.792/0.848; exact set match 66.5% of runs. Smallest model (Granite 4.0 350M) never drained a server in 8 runs. Worst config (Qwen3.5 2B with thinking, leastconn) regressed client 5xx by -667%. Median 5xx reduction 89.6%/93.2% at N=3 vs 77.4%/76.9% at N=9. Recall 0.893 at N=3 to 0.732 at N=9; precision 0.877 to 0.961.
limits: One stack (Flask, Prometheus), up to 9 backends, one fault pattern (every third server has a 5% error rate), self-hosted models. Not a test-selection study.
agent_relevance: With more suspects the agent stays careful about healthy parts but misses faults. Hard caps (drain cap) fire more as the fleet grows.

source: Chauhan and Pendyala (2026) HAProxy: effect of reasoning
finding: Extra reasoning did not improve isolation or the client metric and cost about ten times more output tokens.
numbers: Median 5xx reduction 86.6% no-think vs 86.3% think. GPT-OSS reasoning effort: low 88.5%, medium 88.1%, high 74.0%. Thinking raised median completion tokens per step from 157 to 1,546. Guardrail firing 0.56% of steps at N=3 to 2.38% at N=9.
limits: Same single testbed; within noise except GPT-OSS high effort, where dropped decision steps explain part of the loss.
agent_relevance: Do not buy fault isolation with longer thinking. Spend on a better test choice and a check.

source: Wang and Hong (2025) Time Travel: LLM-Assisted Semantic Behavior Localization with Git Bisect
finding: Binary search over commits (git bisect, O(log n)) with an LLM as the good/bad judge on each diff. Fine-tuning plus chain-of-thought raises end-to-end success.
numbers: 32 curated questions over 3 open-source repos, all-or-nothing success: baseline 74.2% (23/31) to 80.6% (25/31), +6.4 points; paired Wilcoxon p<0.01 over 32 runs. Fine-tune set 30 annotated bisect operations (QLoRA). Self-reported 45.6% less debugging time in a user study.
quote: bisect operation counts as successful only if every step in the sequence of bisect decisions is correct
limits: Very small. One wrong verdict at any step ruins a bisect. Weak on error-handling and safeguard changes. Counts inconsistent (31 vs 32). Time saving self-reported.
agent_relevance: Half-split with a model as the test oracle is fragile because step errors compound. Use a code test as the oracle where possible and verify model verdicts.

source: Wang and Hong (2025) Time Travel: assumptions of bisect
finding: Bisect assumes deterministic tests, monotonic failure and a clean true/false predicate. Flaky tests and non-monotonic regressions break the log n guarantee.
numbers: Under monotonicity the first bad commit is found in O(log n) steps. The paper says the assumptions 'rarely hold' in practice but gives no rate.
limits: Statement from the background section only.
agent_relevance: Half-split needs a single fault and a monotone chain. For branching systems the scaffold needs a functional split, not a linear one.

source: Kim, Chen and Wang (2025) LLM4FL: multi-agent fault localization with graph retrieval and Reflexion
finding: Splits coverage data into ordered divisions (divide and conquer) so each call fits in context, ranks suspicious methods, then a reviewer agent re-checks. Order of divisions matters.
numbers: Defects4J v2.0.0, 675 faults, 14 projects. Top-1 +18.55% over AutoFL and +4.82% over AgentFL (relative gains as printed); prompt chaining raises Top-1 by up to 22%.
limits: Division is a context-fit trick, not an information-gain split. I did not extract the Table 4 ablation numbers. Training-data leakage on Defects4J not tested in what I read.
agent_relevance: Divide-and-conquer over a candidate list is already used inside an LLM loop for software faults; the order of the divisions is a tunable.

source: Microsoft AI (2025) Sequential Diagnosis with Language Models (SDBench, MAI-DxO)
finding: Cost-aware test ordering by a panel of prompted roles on 304 NEJM cases. Same base model, similar or higher accuracy, much less spend when the orchestrator chooses tests under a budget.
numbers: Physicians (21) 19.9% at $2,963; GPT-4o 49.3% at $2,745; o3 78.6% at $7,850; MAI-DxO budgeted 79.9% at $2,396; no-budget 81.9% at $4,735; ensemble 85.5% at $7,184. Single vs batched tests (test set) both 83.9%, $3,991 vs $5,084. Judge kappa 0.70 and 0.87. Average gain about 11 points across model families.
limits: Hidden test set only 56 cases (wide uncertainty). Generalist physicians barred from references. Synthetic findings for tests missing from case text. No healthy patients, so false positives are not measured. US price estimates only.
agent_relevance: Best published example of cost-weighted search in an LLM loop with measured accuracy and spend. Roles: Test-Chooser picks up to three tests that best discriminate hypotheses, Stewardship asks for cheaper equivalents, Challenger tries to falsify, budget tracker cancels tests.

source: Microsoft AI (2025) SDBench: how cost control worked
finding: Savings came from asking cheap questions first and vetoing low-yield expensive tests, not from refusing expensive tests.
numbers: Example: baseline o3 ordered brain MRI and EEG and was wrong at $3,431; MAI-DxO asked about hand sanitizer ingestion, then ran targeted tests, correct at $795. Cost assumptions: $300 per visit, about $0.15 inference per case. Of 508 gatekeeper responses reviewed, 8 were flagged and none leaked the answer.
limits: Single illustrative case. The paper does not quantify how often each role changes the choice and has no per-role ablation in the text read.
agent_relevance: Rule for our scaffold: rank candidate tests by expected information per cost; ask observation questions before instrument tests.

source: Search snippet: DX 2025 'Are Diagnostic Concepts Within the Reach of LLMs?'
finding: Snippet only: tests whether 4o-mini, o1 and o3-mini can generate the model equations (MSOs) used for consistency-based diagnosis on arithmetic and logic circuits.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Not opened. A lead only.
agent_relevance: Links to the subfield on consistency-based diagnosis and conflict generation: can the model produce the conflict sets a half-split needs.

source: Search snippets: OpenRCA (Xu et al., ICLR 2025), AIOpsLab, ORCA-bench
finding: Snippets only: OpenRCA has 335 failures over three enterprise systems and the best model solved 11.34%. AIOpsLab says agents do detection and localization better than root-cause analysis and mitigation. ORCA-bench: best coding agent 25.3% on Medium, 10.0% on Hard.
numbers: 11.34% (OpenRCA); 25.3% and 10.0% (ORCA-bench); all second-hand from a search engine.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Context: machine fault isolation scores on real telemetry are low.

source: Search snippet: SIGMA (2025) AI-Empowered Training Stack on Early-Life Hardware
finding: Snippet: a multi-agent online fault-isolation loop proposes that a node is the cause and queries component metrics to confirm or deny it, a hypothesis-then-measure loop rather than binary search. PDF downloaded; results not read.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Not opened for findings.
agent_relevance: Example of hypothesis-then-measure in production hardware; no half-split evidence.

source: Gap note: no direct LLM half-split study found
finding: Several web searches (half-split, binary search, bisection, delta debugging, measurement selection) found no paper that compares an LLM agent's own test order with a half-split or cost-weighted optimum on a known-fault system, counting tests. Closest are the 20 Questions and Battleship EIG studies, SDBench cost, and git bisect with an LLM oracle.
numbers: Zero direct studies among the sources above.
limits: Absence in my search only; the search tool is limited.
agent_relevance: The comparison 'agent test order vs optimal order on known faults, by number of tests' is a gap our own test can fill.
